overview:
In the study of Jainism, especially within the History and Manuscript Guide mode, the term "shelfmark" refers to the unique identifier assigned to a manuscript, book, or archival unit within a specific library, bhandār (manuscript repository), or institutional collection. Shelfmarks are part of the internal classification system used by custodians to locate, manage, and preserve physical items. They function much like an address: indicating the cupboard, shelf, box, or bundle in which a manuscript is stored, and often encoding additional information such as format, language, or acquisition sequence.

In Jain manuscript culture, shelfmarks are crucial because many important works—canonical āgamas, commentaries, ritual manuals, philosophical treatises, and local histories—survive only in handwritten form in temple libraries, private bhandārs, and public institutions. Scholars working on Jain texts must therefore pay close attention to shelfmarks when citing manuscripts, since the same work may exist in multiple copies across different collections, each with its own local identifier. A typical citation might mention the institution name (for example, a Jain temple library or a university collection), the city, and the shelfmark or accession number, allowing other researchers to trace the exact physical witness used for study.

Shelfmarks are not standardized across all Jain traditions or institutions. Digambara, Śvetāmbara Mūrtipūjaka, Sthānakavāsī, and Terāpanth repositories may each use their own systems, ranging from simple sequential numbers to complex alphanumeric codes. Some older bhandārs rely on traditional labels written on manuscript wrappers or wooden boards, while modern catalogues may assign new shelfmarks linked to digital records. As a result, a single manuscript can sometimes have more than one identifying number: an older local mark and a newer catalogue number. Careful documentation of these variants is an important part of responsible manuscript description.

From a technical perspective, shelfmarks belong to Corpus Tier D (reviewed community education) and C (scholarly cataloguing practice), rather than Tier A primary scripture. They are tools of librarianship and codicology, not religious authorities in themselves. However, they play a vital role in safeguarding access to Tier A and B materials: without reliable shelfmarks, it becomes difficult to verify quotations, compare different manuscript witnesses, or assess the history of a text’s transmission. For students and researchers, learning how to read and use shelfmarks—alongside understanding scripts, colophons, and catalog entries—is a foundational skill in Jain manuscript studies.

In modern practice, shelfmarks are increasingly integrated into digital catalogues and manuscript databases. Institutions may scan or photograph manuscripts and link the digital files to the existing shelfmarks, creating a bridge between physical and virtual collections. This development supports preservation, reduces handling of fragile materials, and allows broader access for scholars worldwide. Yet, even in digital environments, the original shelfmark remains the key reference point for the physical item, ensuring that the manuscript can still be located, conserved, and, when appropriate, ritually respected within its traditional setting.

primary_sources.author: Not applicable (cataloguer-dependent)
primary_sources.translation: Example of how a shelfmark appears in a Jain manuscript catalogue: "Ahmedabad, Jain Bhandār of Shri Nandlal Jain: MS 47/3 (old mark: Kha-12)." Here, "MS 47/3" is the modern shelfmark used by the catalogue, while "Kha-12" is the older local identifier written on the manuscript wrapper. Both are recorded so that the physical item can be reliably located and cross-referenced.
primary_sources.notes: This entry is a schematic illustration rather than a quotation from a canonical Jain text. Shelfmarks themselves are part of library and archival practice, not scriptural doctrine. In Jain studies, they are typically encountered in catalogues, inventories, and scholarly descriptions of manuscripts, which fall under Corpus Tiers C and D. When using such catalogues, students should note the institution name, city, and shelfmark, and, where given, any older local marks or bundle references.

misconceptions.myth: Shelfmarks are religiously authoritative numbers that encode spiritual or karmic meanings in Jainism.
misconceptions.reality: Shelfmarks are practical identifiers used by libraries and bhandārs to locate and manage manuscripts and books. They do not carry doctrinal authority or karmic significance; their purpose is logistical and archival, helping scholars and custodians find specific physical items.

misconceptions.myth: A manuscript without a clear shelfmark is automatically less important or inauthentic.
misconceptions.reality: The absence or ambiguity of a shelfmark usually reflects cataloguing history, not the intrinsic value or authenticity of the text. Many older Jain manuscripts were stored with minimal or informal labeling, and some important works are still being systematically catalogued. Scholarly evaluation relies on the content, script, colophon, and provenance, not solely on the presence of a modern shelfmark.

misconceptions.myth: All Jain institutions follow a single, standardized shelfmark system that can be interpreted the same way everywhere.
misconceptions.reality: Shelfmark systems vary widely between Jain temple libraries, private bhandārs, and public institutions, and across regions and traditions. Codes, numbering schemes, and bundle references are locally defined. Researchers must therefore learn the specific conventions of each collection and consult its catalogue or staff, rather than assuming a universal standard.
